latest_articles.title: News Media, Narrative Authority, and the Global Ordering of Artificial Intelligence
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines how mainstream Western news media structure global hierarchies of technological legitimacy in coverage of artificial intelligence (AI). Although AI circulates worldwide, its public meaning is shaped within a restricted geopolitical and linguistic sphere. Conceptualizing news discourse as a narrative infrastructure that organizes visibility, authority, and technological futurity, we analyze 43,027 English-language newspaper articles from the United States and Europe using computational text analysis combined with interpretive examination. The findings reveal differences in thematic emphasis and actor representation: U.S. coverage frames AI through innovation and economic leadership, European coverage emphasizes regulation and governance, and China appears as a hyper-visible but ambivalent rival associated with surveillance, geopolitical competition, and strategic threat. Actors from Africa and Latin America are largely absent or positioned as sites of implementation, risk, or developmental need. We conceptualize this exclusion as discursive stratification: a hierarchy of narrative inequality in which some actors are positioned as authors of technological futures while others appear as objects, recipients, or peripheral contexts. News discourse thus contributes to the global ordering of technological authority.

latest_articles.title: One-Dimensional Algorithm: Rereading Marcuse’s Critical Theory Through Platform Culture
latest_articles.abstract: This article rereads Herbert Marcuse’s critical theory through algorithmic curation on commercial social media platforms, pursuing a dialectical argument in two directions: first, that platform capitalism structurally reproduces Marcuse’s diagnoses of false needs, incorporation, and one-dimensional thought; second, that platform dynamics exceed his framework—in its passive-subject assumptions, its vagueness about resistance, and its inability to account for the simultaneous production of homogeneity and fragmentation. From this tension, the article develops the concept of algorithmic incorporation: the process by which oppositional thought, practice, and identity enter a platform-mediated cycle of visibility, normalization, commodification, and domestication. Drawing on #BlackLivesMatter as a sustained analytical case, it shows how the four phases operate and specifies observable indicators through which each could be empirically tested. The concept is distinguished from Marcuse’s incorporation, Gramsci’s transformism, and Zuboff’s surveillance capitalism, and corrects accounts—including Bennett and Segerberg’s connective action—that foreground platform infrastructure’s enabling dimensions without reckoning with its costs to movements. Because incorporation operates without a deciding agent, the article concludes, tactical evasion cannot substitute for infrastructural change.

latest_articles.title: Anchored in capital: A Bourdieusian analysis of journalistic identity and resilience in the Portuguese field
latest_articles.abstract: This repeated cross-sectional study (2013-2023) examines the resilience of professional values in Portuguese journalism amid economic precarity and digital disruption. Integrating Bourdieu’s field theory with Raemy’s multi-level identity model, we show how journalists reinforce symbolic capital—intensifying watchdog roles and ethical norms—to preserve field autonomy. Using data from two waves of the Worlds of Journalism Study-Portugal, we analyze how this defensive consolidation operates through capital conversion across macro, meso, and micro levels. The findings reframe value stability not as inertia but as active identity work, offering insights into how peripheral media systems sustain professional coherence under duress.

latest_articles.title: “ In a way, I want TikTok to tell me what I want. . . ” Users’ experience of TikTok as a televisual algorithmic flow
latest_articles.abstract: This article revisits Williams’s concept of flow, Firth’s notion of algorithmic flow, and Picone et al.’s concept of Small Acts of Engagement (SAOE) to examine how users experience TikTok’s algorithmic flow. SAOE are understood as low-effort, everyday acts through which users negotiate their identities and shape their digital consumption. While SAOE have been a valuable lens for understanding user agency on earlier social media platforms, we argue that TikTok’s interface design and cultural framing introduce new challenges. The platform’s design, together with users’ perception of TikTok’s algorithmic flow as a televisual experience, reduces their SAOE to a minimal expression: a rhythm of watch, scroll, repeat , discouraging other forms of intentional, identity-driven engagement. Through a mixed-methods study combining interviews and analysis of participants’ donated TikTok data, we show how our participants experience TikTok as a place for effortless entertainment and continuous consumption, closely resembling the experience of traditional television flow.
affiliations: Centre for Digitalisation, Democracy and Innovation, Brussels School of Governance, Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Brussels, Belgium

latest_articles.title: Prompting with Respect: Cultural Norms and User Experience in LLM Interactions
latest_articles.abstract: Despite growing interest in prompt engineering, its influence on user experience—particularly in relation to cultural communication norms—remains largely unexplored. This controlled experiment examined how respectful versus directive prompting—a culturally meaningful contrast in Korean—affects Korean users’ psychological experience during LLM interactions. Forty-three Korean female college students were randomly assigned to respectful prompt (RP) (using polite requests, compliments, and gratitude) or directive prompt (DP) (using imperatives, criticism, and performance-based penalties) conditions. Participants completed a writing task using ChatGPT. Results indicated that RPs yielded significantly higher satisfaction, particularly for affinity and likability, whereas the difference in perceived output quality was smaller and nonsignificant. Furthermore, RPs elicited socially supportive ChatGPT responses, whereas DPs were followed by apologies, suggesting bidirectional social adaptation between users and ChatGPT. Together, these findings suggest that culturally grounded communicative conventions may shape users’ subjective experience even where perceived output quality does not differ significantly, pointing to culturally adaptive large language model systems that recognize diverse communication patterns as essential design considerations rather than imposing universal paradigms.
affiliations: Department of Psychology, Ewha Womans University, Seoul, Republic of Korea.

latest_articles.title: Dynamic News Visibility Across Media Sources: Evidence from a Chinese Algorithmic Platform
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how recommendation systems organize differential news visibility on Douyin, one of China’s largest short-video platforms. Focusing on the visibility dynamics between government-affiliated media and non-government-affiliated media, the study adopts an agent-based testing (ABT) approach to audit how Douyin’s recommendation system allocates exposure under different stages of user interaction and preference formation. The findings suggest that government-affiliated media receive greater visibility during the early stages of recommendation, when user behavioral data remain limited. However, as recommendation systems accumulate interaction signals over time, non-government-affiliated media gradually gain visibility, particularly under conditions of sustained user engagement. At the same time, the recommendation system does not respond symmetrically to different forms of user preference, revealing varying degrees of algorithmic responsiveness in the visibility allocation process. By examining how recommendation systems negotiate commercial, institutional, and behavioral priorities in news distribution, this study contributes to research on algorithmic visibility, platform governance, and algorithm audit.
affiliations: School of Journalism and Communication, Jinan University

latest_articles.title: Visualizando la Amazonía: Periodismo de Datos, Mapeo y Audiencia del Periodismo Ambiental
latest_articles.abstract: El periodismo ambiental desempeña un papel fundamental en el discurso público, pero enfrenta desafíos para captar audiencias en un panorama mediático digital fragmentado y dominado por grandes empresas tecnológicas. Este estudio explora cómo el periodismo de datos, la entrega personalizada de noticias y las narrativas centradas en la comunidad influyen en el compromiso (engagement) y la confianza de la audiencia en el periodismo ambiental, con un enfoque específico en la región amazónica. A través de una serie de grupos focales con audiencias locales (incluyendo periodistas, investigadores, activistas y ciudadanos interesados), realizados en colaboración con el medio brasileño InfoAmazonia, analizamos las expectativas y hábitos de consumo de la audiencia. Los hallazgos revelan una asincronía significativa entre el periodismo de investigación en profundidad y las preferencias de la audiencia por contenidos concisos y visualmente atractivos, como mapas interactivos y videos cortos. Se demuestra que las visualizaciones de datos aumentan la credibilidad, pero las plataformas digitales funcionan como la principal, aunque algorítmicamente limitada, puerta de acceso a las noticias. Además, las audiencias expresaron una fuerte demanda de mayor representación de voces locales e indígenas, junto con narrativas más orientadas a soluciones. Esta investigación contribuye a la literatura y práctica existentes al ofrecer perspectivas para los medios sobre cómo producir contenido ambiental relevante para las audiencias, abogando por un enfoque periodístico híbrido que equilibre el análisis riguroso de datos con una narrativa accesible y centrada en las personas, con el fin de fomentar un compromiso y una confianza más profundos.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Adult Children’s Chronic Health Conditions and Intergenerational Financial Transfers Between Parents and Early Midlife Adult Children: Variation Across Sons and Daughters
latest_articles.abstract: As our population ages, adult children and parents will experience greater overlap across their lives, offering more opportunities to engage in intergenerational financial transfers. Intergenerational transfers benefit both generations. They may be especially crucial as parents encounter challenges associated with aging, and as adult children grapple with their own health problems. We used the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health data to explore whether an adult child’s chronic health conditions in young adulthood were associated with financial transfers between early midlife adult children and their parents, factoring in differences between sons and daughters. More specifically, we examined the dynamics of upward, downward, and mutual financial transfers among adult children reporting no chronic conditions, one chronic condition, two chronic conditions (multimorbidity), or three or more chronic conditions (severe multimorbidity). Our results indicate adult children with severe multimorbidity were more likely than adult children without chronic health conditions to receive downward financial transfers from their parents. Moreover, adult children with multimorbidity were more likely than adult children without chronic health conditions to engage in mutual financial transfers. Regarding gender of the adult child, we found among children reporting one chronic condition, sons were less likely to engage in downward, upward, and mutual transfers with parents relative to daughters. This research advances our understanding of how an adult child’s chronic health conditions shape dynamics of financial transfers with parents.
affiliations: Department of Sociology, Grand Valley State University

latest_articles.title: Stigma, erasure, and change: Newspaper coverage of prostitution in the mid-20th century
latest_articles.abstract: This project studied news articles about prostitution in the mid-century U.S. to explore the impact of second wave feminism on coverage. Based on a content analysis of 630 articles downloaded from Newspapers.com from the 1950s, ‘60s and ‘70s, it found that while patriarchal values dominated coverage overall, changes could be discerned in the 1970s. Typically, women’s voices were linguistically marginalized even when they were included in coverage. Men, whether as news reporters or as members of law enforcement, were usually the framers of such stories, and when women were included, they were rarely named and quoted far less often. Yet as more women wrote news in the 1970s, stories reflected more concern for women involved in prostitution and were more likely to include their voice. The findings contribute to feminist scholarship and studies of the history of news by underscoring how such coverage, reflected, reinforced, or challenged broader societal hierarchies and power dynamics.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA
The University of Texas at Austin, Philadelphia, PA, USA

latest_articles.title: Don’t Say Values: A Disney Teaching Case
latest_articles.abstract: This case study explores Disney’s response to HB 1557, Florida’s controversial “Don’t Say Gay” bill through the lens of ethically reliable organization theory. CEO Bob Chapek issued a series of statements in response to the bill that received a negative employee response. The dilemma facing Chapek, and employees, revolved around how Disney could maintain ethical reliability when facing internal and external pressure. Organizations that establish an ethically reliable process can benefit by connecting with employees who value ethical standards. But to what extent is an organization then obligated to defend those values and uphold ethical standards in the face of potential retaliation?
affiliations: University of Illinois Urbana Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA

latest_articles.title: Voting for Democracy? Testing Political-Cultural Constraints on Democratic Backsliding
latest_articles.abstract: Democratic backsliding continues to pose a clear danger to contemporary democracies. While a growing literature shows that voters often tolerate antidemocratic candidates when partisan or ideological incentives pull in that direction, we know less about whether support for democracy, institutional trust, political tolerance, and other democratic orientations ameliorate such temptations. We address this question with a systematic comparison of six measures of political culture as predictors of electoral resistance to antidemocratic candidates. Using candidate-choice conjoint experiments fielded in three democracies facing backsliding pressures—the United States, Poland, and South Korea—we find that several democratic orientations are associated with greater resistance to antidemocratic candidates. Among them, support for the core institutions and processes of liberal democracy stands out as the most consistent predictor. Its relationship with prodemocratic choice remains meaningful even in “cross-pressured” choices where partisan or ideological incentives pull voters away from the prodemocratic option. These findings suggest that political culture matters for democratic resilience, though some components of it matter much more consistently than others.
affiliations: Professor of Political Behaviour, School of Social and Political Sciences, University of Glasgow , Glasgow,

latest_articles.title: Interlocking technologies of caste and gender: an interview with Dr. Shailaja Paik
latest_articles.abstract: This interview with MacArthur Fellow and Taft Distinguished Professor of History and Affiliate Faculty in Women’s, Gender, and Sexuality Studies, and Asian Studies Shailaja Paik builds on her insights in the relationship of gender and caste in India to elucidate communications technologies. Paik describes caste as relational in two dimensions, both between communities and within them. She explains her carefully developed methods of historical investigation to analyze the story of women and caste in India, which include drawing on multiple sources in the vernacular Marathi and English, extensive archival documentation, and oral narratives to make nuanced claims about the complicated relationships between caste, class, gender, family, sexuality, citizenship, culture, and educational opportunity. Paik draws on this research to demonstrate a path forward in investigating caste as a communicative technology and communications as signaling caste in multiple ways.

Department of Anthropology, The New School , New York, NY,

latest_articles.title: Interrogating news sources in the Global War on Terror: Kenyan and US journalism's coverage of the 2013 Westgate Mall attack
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how the journalism fields in Kenya and the United States constructed narratives of the 2013 Westgate Mall attack through their news-sourcing practices. Drawing on field theory and j. Siguru Wahutu’s concepts of national and cosmopolitan subfields, the study analyzes how patterns of source selection reflected different journalistic orientations and relationships to the event. A content analysis of 233 articles from leading Kenyan and US news organizations reveals both convergence and divergence in source selection. The Kenyan journalism field relied overwhelmingly on domestic sources (84%), combining state officials (65%) with substantial victim testimony (30%) to frame terrorism as both a security crisis and a collective tragedy. In contrast, the US journalism field prioritized US officials (55%) and experts (20%), while citing Kenyan sources primarily in official roles (40%) that supported the broader “War on Terror” narrative. Despite these differences, both fields ultimately reinforced state-centered interpretations by marginalizing non-elite perspectives and creating a “hierarchy of voice” that sustains dominant war on terror narratives.

latest_articles.title: How to Make Advertising on Social Media Memorable: Stand Out or Get Lost
latest_articles.abstract: This study evaluates the visual salience of static social media ads shown in-feed, identifying the best performing combinations of text- vs. image-based ad creative to different types of visual brand elements. Two online experiments show that image-based ad creative outperforms text-based, gaining higher ad recall, and text-based ad creative reduce correct brand recall. There was also evidence that counterprogramming ad creative type to the type of visual brand elements can overcome some of the disadvantages of text-based ad creative, particularly amongst a brand’s non-buyers and for larger brands. These findings provide insights on how to achieve ad and brand memorability in social media advertising.

latest_articles.title: Diffusion, Logics, and Boundaries: How Journalists in Marginalized Media Markets Negotiate AI in Newsrooms
latest_articles.abstract: Literature on artificial intelligence (AI) and its role in journalism is expanding rapidly. Yet it remains disproportionately focused on Western contexts, ignoring how AI is perceived and negotiated in marginalized or semi-peripheral markets. This article focuses on how journalists in Albania, Croatia, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Romania, Slovenia, and Turkey perceive, apply, and challenge AI technologies. Drawing on theories of diffusion of innovations, institutional logics, and boundary work, this study analyzes the presentation of AI as both a technological innovation and a symbolic threat to professional identity. We conducted 10 focus-group sessions with 68 journalists and editors from diverse media outlets in seven different countries. Sessions were audio-recorded, transcribed, and thematically analyzed. Transcripts were independently coded by two researchers using AI-assisted coding in ATLAS.ti, alongside standard manual coding, with consensus-building to refine the process. The results show skewed and uneven AI implementation, motivated by efficiency requirements and not institutional strategy. Journalists present AI as a helping hand, noting concerns about fact-checking, editorial control, and professional autonomy. These strains indicate conflicting institutional logics, especially between technological efficiency and professional norms, and produce particular kinds of boundary work. Whereas defensive strategies underline the unreliability of human judgment, adaptive strategies also incorporate AI under editorial oversight. The article is relevant to the literature because it emphasizes ways in which structural limitations, institutional stresses, and professional ideals influence AI adoption outside of Western media systems.

latest_articles.title: Giving AI a Body: Representations of Social Robots in Latin American Media
latest_articles.abstract: Social robots (physically embodied systems designed to interact with humans through social behaviours) have gained increasing visibility in news media. However, their everyday presence in Latin America remains limited, reflecting broader asymmetries in technological diffusion across non-WEIRD contexts. This study examines how social robots are represented in Latin American news media and how artificial intelligence (AI) is communicated through embodied technologies. A quantitative content analysis was conducted on a corpus of 404 news articles published in Spanish and Portuguese language media, retrieved through Google’s search engine. The study employs an LLM-assisted coding procedure combining automated classification with human validation. The analysis focuses on three dimensions: journalistic treatment (narrative frames and evaluative tone), representation of AI (attributed agency and explicit references to AI), and social functions (social roles, sectors of application, and sources). The findings show that coverage is predominantly framed around care and assistance, with positive or ambivalent evaluations, while conflict-oriented frames remain marginal. Social robots are mainly portrayed as assistants or caregivers, described as semiautonomous systems, and situated in healthcare and research contexts. Coverage relies largely on corporate and scientific sources, with a limited presence of civic or governmental voices. These representations position social robots as a key interface through which AI becomes publicly interpretable. The study contributes to research on AI and journalism in non-WEIRD contexts by showing how media representations shape understanding of emerging technologies in the absence of widespread direct experience.

latest_articles.title: Makeup Activism on TikTok: Beauty as Political and Visibility Work Under Platformization
latest_articles.abstract: Social media platforms increasingly shape how activism emerges and operates. Within these attention economies, visibility is a crucial but unevenly distributed resource, structured both by platform infrastructures and gendered power relations. This article examines how feminist actors negotiate these conditions on TikTok by mobilizing beauty practices—specifically makeup—as platform-specific resources for political expression. Focusing on two distinct cases, the Iranian #WomanLifeFreedom movement and the Latin American #NiUnaMenos protests against feminicides, the study analyzes 200 TikTok videos through comparative multimodal discourse analysis. Despite major differences in political context and risk, activists across both cases converge in their use of shared visibility strategies: They adapt TikTok’s dominant beauty formats, including makeup tutorials, transformation videos, and facial inscription, to embed feminist critique within familiar, algorithmically favored genres. By repurposing practices traditionally associated with beautification and commodification, creators transform makeup into a visual repertoire of resistance. Conceptualized here as makeup activism, these practices allow feminist content to circulate through high-visibility platform vernaculars. The article argues that visibility on TikTok is not simply a matter of exposure, but a strategic and contested resource shaped by the interaction of platform infrastructures, aesthetic conventions, and gendered politics. In doing so, it contributes to feminist media studies by moving beyond a focus on representation and providing empirical evidence on how feminist actors strategically negotiate gendered regimes of visibility across platformed public spheres that span diverse national and transnational settings.

latest_articles.title: Greening Mobile AI?
latest_articles.abstract: Mobile AI is very much a work in progress. No better time at the outset, then, to consider its environmental implications. As mobile media and communication are woven together with AI, what are their entanglements—and what are the implications for the environment? First, given the slow progress on concerted effort over many years to tackle reuse, repair and ‘greening’ of mobile phones, as well as other mobile technology devices, and associated information and communication technologies, and the research and critique engaging with this endeavour—it is critical to consider the best focus as we move into the AI phone and beyond-the-phone future. Second, the article dissects key trends and issues—hot spots—in the environmental implications of the wider networks, infrastructures, systems and ecologies where mobiles and AI are being deployed in combination—but their ecological implications deserve greater attention. Third, the article proposes priority elements for the research and policy agenda in greening mobile AI.

latest_articles.title: Unfinished Revenge: (Un)Popular Feminism, Class Politics, and Women’s Rage in Contemporary Chinese Television
latest_articles.abstract: This paper examines recent Chinese televisual portrayals of women’s revenge against men who abuse their gender privileges afforded by patriarchy. Focusing on two recent women-centered Chinese dramas as case studies, I interrogate how women’s revenge against male villains is represented on television and received by audiences. I characterize both narratives as “unfinished,” insofar as structural gender injustice is rendered visible and questioned but not dismantled through women-led revenge. Online audience comments express resentment at this very incompleteness, thereby problematizing the popular feminist promise of happiness. At the same time, feminist rage against gender injustice becomes entangled with grievances at fictional characters, cast members, and other marginalized groups in reality. By critically examining targets of women’s rage on and off the screen, I suggest that feminist scholar should not treat rage as a monolithic or inherently politically productive affect, but rather be cautious about its potential appropriation for non-emancipatory ends.

latest_articles.title: ‘That’s not a quirk of racism [. . .] – that’s a quirk of geography’: Exploring the role of place(s) in assigning responsibility for exclusion in grassroots cricket in Australia
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines how place is discursively constructed as an agent in talk about the exclusion of ethnic minority players in Australian grassroots cricket. Drawing on 40 semi-structured interviews with players and other stakeholders, we combine thematic analysis with Critical Discourse Analysis to identify the linguistic strategies used to construct place(s). We show how references to places of different degrees of granularity – from very specific to more general – shift responsibility for exclusion away from individuals and organisations, attributing it instead to geography. This discursive framing constructs exclusion as natural, inevitable, and beyond human intervention, thereby obscuring accountability and limiting the potential for meaningful change. By foregrounding references to place as a mechanism through which exclusion is normalised and justified, the article advances sociolinguistic understandings of how language shapes experiences of belonging and marginalisation in sport. The study highlights the need to critically examine spatial discourses when addressing inequalities in sport.

latest_articles.title: Exposure to “connective language” in political Facebook posts leads to more enjoyment and less psychological reactance
latest_articles.abstract: In this preregistered study, we experimentally tested (n = 2,032) whether “connective language”—language that expresses openness to others’ perspectives and humility in presenting one’s viewpoints—reduces psychological reactance to disagreeable political messages. Compared with non-connective Facebook posts, a single connective post reduced expressed reactance, counter-arguing, and perceived threat to one’s freedom. Connective posts also elicited fewer negative and positive emotions. Participants found connective posts more enjoyable and they spent more time reading them, although these posts were slightly longer. However, post type did not affect behavioral engagement, such as liking or replying. Our findings suggest that social media platforms should optimize their algorithms to surface connective language, and the public should consider adopting this type of language.

latest_articles.title: Communicating, Interacting and Strategizing: Exploring the Situatedness of Strategy-Making
latest_articles.abstract: While a growing body of work has established that strategy is communicatively constituted through talk, writing, narratives, documents, material artifacts and multimodal interactions, this literature remains dispersed across disciplinary traditions and publication outlets. This special issue transcends such boundaries and brings together contributions that foreground the communicative and interactional accomplishment of strategizing, to demonstrate what is gained when researchers attend to how people collectively define, negotiate and enact strategic concerns in situated contexts. Articles in the special issue examine strategizing across a diverse range of settings, including entrepreneurial ventures, social movements, digital collaboration platforms, organizational restructuring processes and political organizing. They show how strategic action emerges through situated communicative practices and engage with key concerns in organization studies, including authority, materiality and entrepreneurship. Attending to the situatedness of communication enriches Strategy-as-Practice research and related traditions, opening new avenues for investigating strategizing in increasingly mediated, fluid and pluralistic organizational environments.
affiliations: Department of Humanities, Letters and Communication, Université TÉLUQ, Montréal, QC, Canada

latest_articles.title: Story-Driven Insights: How Transitional Characters and Positive Role Models in Video Narratives Shape Outgroup Attitudes
latest_articles.abstract: This study presents results of a pre-registered online experiment (N = 927) examining the persuasive effects of professionally produced video narratives aimed at reducing anti-immigrant prejudice. Drawing on narrative persuasion and inspiring media frameworks, we tested how protagonist type—positive role model versus transitional character—shapes identification and activates psychological insight, a transformative cognitive response linked to attitude change. A 3 (character type: control or non-confrontation condition, transitional character, positive role model) × 3 (stereotype type: “immigration increases crime,” “immigrants take our jobs,” “immigrants receive excessive public assistance”) between-subjects design was employed. Participants viewed audiovisual narratives depicting a dramatized incident in which a negative stereotype about immigrants was introduced and either confronted by the protagonist or left unaddressed (non-confrontation condition). After exposure, identification, psychological insight, and outcome variables were measured. The results showed that modern racism moderated the effects of character type on identification: low-prejudice individuals identified more strongly with the positive role model, whereas high-prejudice individuals reported lower identification in both experimental conditions. Identification predicted psychological insight, which in turn mediated outcomes (story liking, willingness to share, and outgroup attitudes). These findings indicate that video narratives can elicit character-driven insight and foster inclusive attitudes among receptive audiences, advancing understanding of how entertainment-education can counter prejudice.

latest_articles.title: Do Emotional Ads Persuade? Evidence from Real-Time Campaign Advertising Experiments
latest_articles.abstract: We evaluate whether campaign advertisements that generate larger emotional reactions also generate larger persuasive effects in contemporary elections. We analyze 29 weeks of experiments conducted during the 2016 U.S. presidential campaign, in which 48 authentic campaign ads were tested in real time, often within days of their debut. The ads and a placebo were randomly assigned to approximately 28,000 subjects. We find that campaign ads reliably move emotions, albeit in largely partisan ways, with comparatively muted reactions among independents. Critically, however, these emotional reactions do not predict the magnitude of an ad’s effect on candidate favorability, vote intention, policy preferences, or turnout intention. Our results cast doubt on emotion-based accounts of advertising persuasion in polarized elections and caution practitioners against using self-reported emotional reactions as a measure of message effectiveness.

latest_articles.journal: Annals of the International Communication Association
latest_articles.title: Encrypted politics in the Global South: a decolonial systematic review of WhatsApp and political communication
latest_articles.abstract: This article presents a systematic review of scholarly research on the political uses of WhatsApp, with a particular focus on studies conducted in or about the Global South. While research on digital politics has largely centered on open, platform-visible spaces such as Twitter and Facebook, WhatsApp constitutes a distinct political communication environment: encrypted, mobile-first, and shaped by vernacular practices that complicate visibility, data access, and governance. Drawing on a dataset of 239 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2016 and 2024 and indexed in Scopus, the review maps dominant themes, methodological approaches, geographic distributions, and patterns of authorship and collaboration in the field. The findings show that scholarship has overwhelmingly focused on misinformation, elections, and activism, often framing WhatsApp primarily through risk, harm, and regulation. In contrast, everyday political communication, participatory vernaculars, democratic affordances, and the mundane political uses of encrypted messaging remain comparatively underexplored. Methodologically, the literature is skewed toward surveys and content analysis, with limited use of ethnographic, critical, or computational approaches capable of engaging encrypted environments on their own terms. The review also reveals persistent structural asymmetries in knowledge production, including disparities in funding, institutional affiliation, collaboration patterns, language of publication, and epistemic authority, particularly between Global North institutions and Global South research contexts. Adopting a decolonial perspective, the article argues that the study of encrypted messaging platforms requires methodological and epistemological approaches attentive to opacity, infrastructural inequality, and locally grounded political practice. By theorizing the political affordances of encrypted communication and identifying key empirical and conceptual blind spots, the review contributes to debates in political communication and platform studies while positioning the Global South as a site of theoretical and methodological innovation rather than merely empirical application.
affiliations: Centre for Film and Media Studies, University of Cape Town , Cape Town,

latest_articles.title: Fabulating the Environmental Villain: Technocultures, African Cultural Rhetorics and Community Literacies of Ecological Justice in the #StopGalamseyNow Campaign
latest_articles.abstract: At the interstices of critical African communication studies, digital cultural rhetorics, and community literacy studies, we theorize how galamsey actors are rhetorically fabulated as environmental villains within Ghanaian protest rhetorics. Through a rhetorical discourse analysis of posts collected during the #StopGalamseyNow campaign, this paper traces how anthropocentrism, moral culpability, and community literacies of ecological kinship are discursively communicated in Ghanaian digital culture. In attending to the rhetorical valences of activist discourses, we ground our analysis in ukama, a Shona relational philosophy which emphasizes kinship, care, and multispecies stewardship. Our analysis traces rhetorical motifs of biophilia, ecocentrism, and ancestricide discursivities through which galamsey actors are sculpted as ‘unsavoury' threats to Ghana’s land, water, and national futures. We argue that such intrepid technocultural activism enacts a praxis of environmental fracturization, which renders galamsey actors as communal villains, while topicalizing triad structures of political complicity, neoliberal extractive governance, and clandestine galamsey networks. More importantly, the reticularity of protest rhetorics pushes us to advocate for a dialectical synergy between digital authorship of ecological justice and offline, place-based activism toward just ecological futures. By foregrounding African environmental epistemologies, this study thus extends global conversations on environmental humanities, cultural rhetorics, and ecoliteracy.

latest_articles.title: Remediation Practices in Environmental Communication: The Case of the Chilean Civil Organisations
latest_articles.abstract: Digital communication has significantly transformed communicative practices, offering affordances and advantages previously unattainable through earlier technologies. Among these, remediation (understood as the transfer of content from one medium to another) emerges as a fundamental and widespread practice. This study investigates the use of remediation by environmental organizations in their efforts to construct and defend public narratives on behalf of nature within politicized contexts. Employing a mixed-methods approach, the research analyses visual content (n = 1,736) published on Instagram by ten Chilean environmental organizations, alongside in-depth interviews with their producers. Findings reveal a complex structure of remediation practices, regarded by most organizations as integral to contemporary environmental advocacy. This article proposes a typology of remediation based on four analytical dimensions: media-meaning-dimension, source-realm-dimension, source-closeness-dimension, and function-dimension. Additionally, it examines the strategic role of third-party branding within remediation practices, highlighting its relevance in enhancing legitimacy, visibility, and discursive influence.

latest_articles.title: The labour of girlhood innocence: Shirley Temple, Hu Rongrong, and the genealogy of child stardom in 1930s trans-pacific visual culture
latest_articles.abstract: Child stars are both children and cross-cultural visual figures whose identities are shaped by the film industry. From a trans-Pacific perspective, this study compares two representative female child stars from the 1930s: Shirley Temple in the United States and Hu Rongrong in China. By focusing on these two highly interconnected figures, it asks how girlhood innocence is gendered in different industrial contexts, how it is transformed by visual media into an emotional resource for adult audiences, and how it becomes a transpacific consumable cultural product. The article argues that girlhood innocence shown in cinema is not an inherent quality, but a gendered performance produced through cinematic visual representation and consumer culture. In the United States, within the context of the Hollywood studio system, Temple is valued for providing emotional reassurance through “cuteness” and innocence. In China, within Shanghai’s semi-colonial film industry, Hu Rongrong reproduces “the Temple model” and embodies the public desire for urban modernity. Through a close visual and contextual comparison, this study further interrogates the moral ambivalence surrounding female child stars, particularly regarding their emotional labour and the inadequate protections afforded to them, issues that continue to resonate in contemporary forms of children’s exposure on media platforms.
affiliations: China University of Political Science and Law

latest_articles.title: Effective Messaging Against Youth E-Cigarette Use: Does Humor Make a Difference?
latest_articles.abstract: Anti-vaping campaigns have the potential to reduce youth e-cigarette use in the United States. It is unclear how humor, a common feature in youth anti-tobacco communication, affects intended and unintended message outcomes and interacts with message themes and youth rebelliousness. We conducted a mixed between- and within-subjects experiment using an online convenience sample of 13–17-year-old non-current e-cigarette users (N = 1,366). Participants were randomized to view anti-vaping public service announcement (PSA) ads with humorous text and humorous imagery (HH), humorous text and non-humorous imagery (HN), or non-humorous text and non-humorous imagery (NN). Within each condition, participants viewed five images. The five images represented five themes identified in previous literature as highly effective (i.e., health effects and chemicals) and less effective (i.e., flavors, industry manipulation, mental health). Linear mixed effects models explored main effects of message condition on intended effects (i.e., perceived message effectiveness, message liking, amusement, and worry) and unintended effects (i.e., reactance, anger, perceived message credibility, and susceptibility to e-cigarettes), and additionally tested interactions with theme and youth rebelliousness. Eighty-six percent of the sample were susceptible to e-cigarette use at baseline. Main effects indicated lower perceived message effectiveness (PME) and ad liking for the HN compared to the NN condition (p < .05). Ads in the HH condition elicited higher amusement compared to the NN condition (p < .05). Significant interactions were observed between theme and condition for PME and messaging liking. Interactions between condition and youth rebelliousness were not significant. PSAs with both humorous text and imagery performed similarly to non-humorous messages and did not result in unintended consequences, a finding that can support the use of humor as a variation in message strategy in anti-vaping campaigns. Humor, however, may decrease perceived effectiveness and liking relative to non-humorous messages when paired with lower effectiveness themes. Pilot testing of humorous anti-vaping PSAs may be needed prior to dissemination.
affiliations: Rutgers Institute for Nicotine & Tobacco Studies

latest_articles.title: Prenatal Genetic Testing on TikTok: Lay Narratives and Expertise
latest_articles.abstract: In recent years, social-media platforms have seen a rise in content related to pregnancy "gender reveals," wherein parents-to-be draw from the results of NIPT (noninvasive prenatal testing) to disclose the "gender" of their fetus. Such reveals are grounded in inaccurate understandings of NIPT as a technology and its relationship to fetal sex or gender information, understandings that can perpetuate harms for parents-to-be and infants alike. To explore where these understandings come from and how they are communicated, this study offers a thematic, narrative analysis of 40 recent TikTok videos posted by lay individuals discussing both NIPT and fetal sex chromosomes, sex, and/or gender. Findings reveal that almost all videos upheld both a diagnostic myth about NIPT (that the test is diagnostic rather than a probabilistic screening) and a conflation myth (wherein sex and gender are considered equivalent concepts). Videos fell into one of three narrative themes (i.e., personal storytelling; educational framing; co-storytelling), which were made persuasive by specific configurations of lay expertise (i.e., experiential; hybrid; relational, respectively). These results extend predominant theories of lay expertise by identifying and operationalizing distinct forms of lay expertise at work in the context of health communication on social media.

latest_articles.title: Examining the Mediating Effects of Mutuality and Openness in the Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Public Relations Practice: A Predictive PLS-SEM Approach
latest_articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly transforming public relations (PR), with implications for dialogic communication and relationship cultivation. Although its transformative potential has been widely theorized, empirical evidence remains limited, particularly in Global South contexts. This study surveyed 398 Kenyan PR practitioners to examine (i) whether GAI adoption influences organization-public dialogic communication (OPDC) principles, mutuality and openness, and (ii) whether AI-enhanced OPDC mediates relational outcomes, specifically trust and satisfaction. Using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), the findings indicate that all hypothesized relationships are positive and statistically significant. The coefficients of determination (R2) demonstrate substantial explanatory power and predictive relevance. Moreover, mutuality and openness exhibit complementary (partial) mediation effects, indicating that GAI enhances relational outcomes both directly and indirectly through strengthened dialogic communication. These results position GAI not merely as a technological tool but as a structurally influential factor in contemporary organization-public relationship management. The study contributes to PR scholarship by empirically integrating GAI into dialogic communication theory and offers practical insights for practitioners navigating AI-enabled communication environments.

latest_articles.title: How Memes Reconfigure the Communicative Codes of Luxury Branding: Participatory Digital Culture and the Shift of Symbolic Authority
latest_articles.abstract: This study explores how internet memes, as participatory cultural artifacts, disrupt and redefine luxury brand communication. Drawing on in-depth interviews and visual analysis of memes, we examine how meme culture reconfigures Gurzki, Schlatter, and Woisetschläger’s (Citation2019) principles of enrichment, distancing, and abstraction. Findings reveal three interlinked shifts: a symbolic shift, reframing luxury meanings through parody and depletion of symbolic complexity; a social shift, positioning meme creators as new cultural intermediaries; and a commercial shift, in which brands cautiously engage with meme culture. This research advances understanding of digital cultural production and its impact on symbolic capital in the luxury field.
affiliations: TU Braunschweig, Institute of Marketing & Innovation

latest_articles.title: A culture-centered exploration of mental health among predominantly South Asian second-generation immigrant women in the United States
latest_articles.abstract: Using a culture-centered approach (CCA), this study examined the mental health experiences of predominantly South Asian second-generation immigrant women in the United States. Specifically, it explored how participants made sense of, negotiated, and navigated mental health within immigrant households in the United States. Drawing on 23 semi-structured, in-depth interviews with women aged 18–43, the study identified two interrelated communication processes: navigating structural conditions and negotiating cultural meanings of mental health, and enacting agency through strategic communicative practices. Findings reveal that participants experienced misalignment between available services and lived needs, shaped by barriers such as cost, representation, and language, as well as by community and family norms that regulate disclosure. At the same time, participants enacted agency through strategic communicative practices, including selective disclosure, peer support, and negotiated family engagement. Across the two communication processes, silence functioned as both a constraint on disclosure and a strategic resource for managing relational risk, while agency was enacted through everyday communicative practices rather than solely through overt resistance. The findings suggest that mental health interventions for immigrant women should move toward co-created, structurally responsive approaches that center lived experience.

latest_articles.title: Addressing communication barriers to public understanding of climate change in selected coastal communities in Ghana
latest_articles.abstract: A major obstacle to combating climate change lies in bridging the gap between communication and the required public involvement. Using convergent parallel mixed-methods and informed by Afrocentric theory, we conducted surveys, interviews, and focus group discussions with residents and community leaders in selected coastal communities across Ghana’s Western and Central Regions. The study aimed to identify obstacles impeding the public understanding of climate-related information, their impact on adaptation efforts, and strategies to enhance climate communication. The findings revealed that language barriers, lack of education, and mistrust in climate information hinder the audience's comprehension of climate messaging. These obstacles result in limited adaptation knowledge, little or no effort to adapt, destruction due to unannounced disasters, and poor living conditions. The study also revealed some community-level strategies for enhancing climate change communication, including the use of alternative media, highlighting solutions, and public education on climate change, which could spur the necessary engagement. Findings from this study offer a model for improving climate communication strategies in similar vulnerable regions, ultimately contributing to more effective and inclusive climate change adaptation efforts in Ghana and beyond.

latest_articles.title: Loneliness and the local news environment
latest_articles.abstract: Recent research suggests that changes to the media environment have contributed to loneliness in the United States. This work focuses on smartphones and social media, with the decline of local news receiving little attention. We argue that local news promotes social well-being by informing residents about their communities, fostering attachment and a sense of belonging that can reduce loneliness. We provide evidence in two studies. First, using state-level data and multiple measures of news availability, we show that loneliness is higher in states with fewer options for local news. Second, we find in a nationally representative survey that people who rarely consume local journalism report greater loneliness than regular local news consumers. There is some evidence that the relationship is strongest in rural areas, which have experienced severe declines in local news access. We conclude by proposing a research agenda to further explore how community news may support social well-being.
affiliations: George Washington University Department of Political Science, , Washington, DC,

latest_articles.title: Looking good, fitting in: co-trajectories of appearance- and friendship-related identity distress and positive online self-presentation in adolescence
latest_articles.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period for identity development, often accompanied by identity distress. Simultaneously, adolescents are also preoccupied with presenting themselves as positive as possible on social media, which may reflect and reinforce identity distress. Yet, the dynamic associations between adolescents’ identity distress and positive online self-presentations remain unexplored. Accordingly, this three-wave panel study among adolescents from Belgium, France, and Slovenia (N = 1,697; Mage = 15.14, SDage = 1.78, 57.2% girls) used Latent Class Growth Analysis to identify distinct co-trajectories of identity distress and positive online self-presentation in the domains of friendship and appearance over one year. The findings showed that identity distress and positive self-presentations can follow maladaptive, (high risk) adaptive, or stable co-trajectories over time, depending on the identity domain, adolescents’ demographic, and social media use characteristics. In doing so, the study provides novel evidence on the heterogeneous co-development of adolescents’ identity distress and online self-presentation.
affiliations: Media Psychology Lab, Department of Communication Sciences, Faculty of Social Sciences, KU Leuven , Leuven,

latest_articles.title: Liking Fast-Food Brands Predicts Poorer Diet Quality, Independent of Perceived Healthiness
latest_articles.abstract: Within the theory of planned behavior, ambivalent attitudes (that are simultaneously positive and negative) can weaken the link between attitudes, intentions and behavior. This study examined whether perceived healthiness of fast-food brands would weaken the relationship between positive emotional attitudes toward fast-food brands and diet quality. In Study 1, university students in Australia completed the study in a lab; Study 2 (pre-registered) was completed by US-based participants online. In both experiments, participants rated major fast food and beverage brand logos on liking and perceived healthiness, completed dietary questionnaires (DFS, RED-13) and self-reported BMI and demographic data. Sensitivity analyses excluded brands marketed as "healthy." Consistently across both Australian and American samples, dietary fat and sugar intake was predicted by both higher liking ratings of fast-food brand logos and reward-based eating styles. Contrary to expectations, these effects were not significantly moderated by perceived healthiness of the brands. Fast-food brands that were more liked were also perceived to be healthier by those consuming more dietary fat and sugar. These results point to a possible contribution of food brand marketing and brand loyalty in shaping consumer behavior.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Keeping and Deleting Messages in Ongoing Romantic Relationships: Extending the Virtual Relationship Memory Model
latest_articles.abstract: People frequently decide which virtual objects (e.g., messages, photos) exchanged with romantic partners to keep or delete. The virtual relationship memory model (VRMM) argues these decisions help shape relational memories and meaning. However, the model was developed in the context of relationship dissolution. The present study extends the VRMM to the context of ongoing romantic relationships. Specifically, this study consisted of 30 semi-structured interviews with adults who reported on their motivations for keeping or deleting virtual objects, the perceived consequences of such decisions, and the ways in which network members influence their decision processes. Findings showed that participants kept virtual objects as relational memory resources and for partner accountability, whereas deletion served emotion regulation, conflict management, impression management, and privacy functions. Deletion created uncertainty within the relationship depending on message content and relational context, and network members influenced message management choices. By extending the VRMM to ongoing relationships, this study reframes virtual relational memory not only as a retrospective account of past relationships, but also as an ongoing communicative process. Additionally, it identifies motivations and consequences of message management unique to intact relationships.
affiliations: School of Communication Studies, University of Tennessee

latest_articles.title: “X is simply broken”: The relationship between political journalists and politicians on social media during the 2025 German federal election campaign
latest_articles.abstract: Contemporary election campaigns are marked by a move from political parties and politicians to communicating directly to audiences via social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and TikTok. In doing so, they deliberately bypass journalistic rigour and scrutiny to focus on more personal messages and storytelling techniques. Scholarship has investigated this from the perspective of social media platform logics and political campaigning but has thus far somewhat neglected the journalistic dimension. Using the case study of the snap German federal elections held in February 2025, this contribution features expert interviews with a diverse range of German political journalists and investigates their perspectives on a) how leading politicians used social media platforms in their campaigns and b) how they use said platforms themselves for news sourcing and diffusion as well as direct communication with politicians. Findings reveal a shift away from X (formerly Twitter) and a stronger focus on more outspoken audiovisual platforms such as TikTok for news sourcing and diffusion purposes, while ascribing growing relevance to LinkedIn and even traditional text messages. Politicians’ messages are perceived as steering away from overt political messages, feeding into the ongoing debate about the depoliticization of political communication.

latest_articles.title: Intrapreneurial Practices in News Media Organisations: A Multi-level Analysis
latest_articles.abstract: News media organisations are under constant pressure to innovate and renew themselves. Under these conditions, intrapreneurship offers a way to advance innovation from within existing organisations by enabling employees to initiate, develop, and promote new ideas as part of their everyday work. This article examines how intrapreneurial practices support innovation in journalism and media work. Drawing on a practice-based, multi-level framework, the study analyses intrapreneurial activity at individual, team, and organisational levels in two Finnish news media companies. Based on a dual-case study of semi-structured interviews with media managers, the analysis examines concrete episodes that explain how intrapreneurial activity is initiated, advanced, and supported in journalism and media work. The findings show how intrapreneurial activity is enacted through interconnected practices across levels and depends on surrounding organisational conditions. The article offers a systematic way to analyse intrapreneurial activity in journalism and offers practical insights for news media professionals and organisations seeking renewal by showing how innovation is put into practice in everyday media work.
affiliations: Department of Management Studies, Aalto University School of Business, Espoo, Finland
VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland, Espoo, Finland

latest_articles.title: From Detection to Counterspeech: Auditing AI Moderation and Fact-Checking Practices in Ethiopia’s Multilingual Online Sphere
latest_articles.abstract: AI-assisted content moderation promises to manage online incivility at scale while sparing human moderators traumatic content. Yet most evidence comes from Western languages and contexts. This study examines how AI hate-speech detection interacts with counterspeech and fact-checking in Ethiopia’s polarized Amharic and Afan Oromo spaces. Drawing on infrastructural invisibility and civic labor, it triangulates a computational audit of three classifiers against 838 hand-annotated posts (2020–2025), document analysis of platform self-descriptions and transparency reports, and 20 interviews with Ethiopian fact-checkers, volunteer flaggers, and counter-speakers. The most widely used generic classifier cannot read either language natively and, on English translations, recovers only about a tenth of hate speech; locally-oriented classifiers perform far better on Amharic but collapse on Afan Oromo, leaving it effectively unserved. Across every tool, the dominant error is under-detection, not over-removal, and the same silence recurs in platforms’ self-descriptions. Rather than sparing anyone the work, AI’s failure displaces it onto an unpaid volunteer ecology that absorbs political and psychological costs platforms benefit from yet refuse to name.

latest_articles.title: From defiance to distortion: misappropriation of gendered resistance in two cases of protests in northeast India
latest_articles.abstract: This essay interrogates the symbolic and political trajectories of two gendered protests in Northeast India—Manipur’s 2004 Kangla Fort naked protest and Assam’s 2023 Silsako semi-nude protest—to examine how acts of embodied defiance are systematically misappropriated by patriarchal state and media narratives. Drawing on postcolonial feminist theory and critical discourse analysis, the paper argues that while such protests deploy nakedness as a subversive tactic to reclaim agency and challenge state violence, their radical potential is often diluted through eroticisation, sensationalism, and narrative reframing. These protests become visual spectacles, displaced from their political roots and repurposed into consumable, depoliticised media events. The essay argues this process as a “boomerang effect,” wherein feminist resistance is reabsorbed into the very structures of power it aims to disrupt. Through a comparative analysis of media framings, symbolic strategies, and socio-political reception, the study highlights how gendered resistance is differentially legitimised based on caste, region, and militarisation. Ultimately, the essay calls for praxis-oriented feminist strategies that resist co-optation, foreground structural injustice, and reassert narrative agency. It contributes to broader debates on the neoliberal commodification of dissent, proposing that meaningful feminist resistance must transcend spectacle and align with legal, media, and activist interventions that uphold political intent.

latest_articles.title: The Use of Social Media in Health Interventions for People Living with Cancer: A Systematic Review
latest_articles.abstract: Social media offers scalable opportunities for social connection and health communication; however, its role in cancer interventions remains unclear. This systematic review examines the use of social media in cancer-related health interventions and their targeted outcomes. The review was registered with PROSPERO and conducted according to the PRISMA guidelines. Seven databases were searched for English-language randomized controlled trials (RCTs) (2000-2024) evaluating cancer interventions with a social media component. Eligible studies involved adults (≥18 years) with a cancer diagnosis and reported outcomes related to physical, psychological, or social well-being. Intervention characteristics were categorized by social media role, intended effects, and platform affordances. Seventeen RCTs were included. Quality of life was the most assessed outcome, with frequent improvements in psychosocial measures (e.g., anxiety, depression, and social support) and some physical benefits (e.g., fatigue, pulmonary function, and daily step count). WeChat was the dominant social media platform, followed by Facebook. Most interventions delivered education, social support, and disease management, although few studies measured actual platform usage. The reported effects were shaped by common platform affordances, flexibility, structure, adaptation, narration, and identity, which enabled private communication, real-time clinician support, narrative sharing, and tailored guidance. Findings suggest that social media platforms can enhance well-being, self-management, and social support for people living with cancer when these features are intentionally aligned with communication and behavior-change mechanisms. This review underscores the importance of theory-informed, context-specific design, rather than assuming benefit from social media use alone.
affiliations: Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications

latest_articles.title: Crisis Leadership in Public Relations: Examining the Roles of Ethics Resources, Equity Support, and Crisis Communication Effectiveness in the Pandemic Crisis
latest_articles.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has generated a significant impact on several aspects of public relations practice. By focusing on crisis leadership, this study explores mediating effects of public relations (PR) practitioners’ work challenges, ethics resources, equity support, and crisis communication effectiveness on their crisis leadership perceptions. An online survey was conducted to investigate 1,044 PR practitioners, with 42.7% having more than 10 years of professional experience, followed by 32.5% with 6–10 years, and 24.8% with less than 5 years of experience. Results suggest that all three factors, including ethics resources, equity support, and crisis communication effectiveness, generate significant effects on crisis leadership perceptions. Specifically, PR practitioners’ perceived ethics resources and equity support mediate direct effects of their work challenge on their crisis leadership perceptions, yet their perceived crisis communication effectives can further intervene indirect effects of their ethics resources and equity support on their crisis leadership perceptions. This study contributes to an understanding of strategic communication practices during the pandemic crisis by examining PR practitioners’ crisis leadership perceptions and further illuminates the values of these dynamic factors as key mediators that do not only decrease PR practitioners’ work challenge but also strengthen their crisis leadership perceptions.

latest_articles.title: How Platform Affordances Shape Expression Effects: Comment Length and Audience in Political News Engagement
latest_articles.abstract: This experiment (N = 775) examined how commenting affordances shape expression effects in political news. Participants were assigned to conditions that varied comment length (short vs. long) and audience type (private, public, ingroup, or outgroup) on a simulated news platform. Composition and release affordances interacted rather than operating independently: short ingroup-directed comments were associated with less anger and greater enthusiasm, whereas longer private comments heightened affective polarization relative to public ones. A computational linguistic analysis revealed distinct word-use patterns across conditions. Findings establish the contingent structure of expression effects and advance a mass–interpersonal–intrapersonal framework, with implications for news platform design.
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong

latest_articles.title: The power of conversational writing style: Examining the influence of sourcing and writing style on credibility in community journalism
latest_articles.abstract: This article revisits the issue of the credibility of citizen journalism in the context of community news. By unpacking its two major reporting characteristics — sourcing from citizens and conversational writing style — this study contributes to our understanding of what makes citizen journalism trustworthy. A 2 (sourcing: elite vs citizen) × 2 (writing style: conversational vs professional) between-subjects experiment ( N = 311) was conducted in Taiwan in late January 2024. Results showed that conversational writing style was considered more credible and more narratively transported than professional journalistic writing. Besides, media skepticism moderated the relationship between conversational writing style and narrative transportation. This implies that, at least concerning community topics, conversational writing style emerges as the critical factor enabling citizen journalism to win trust among the public. Furthermore, results suggest a need to reconsider the rigid professional journalistic norms in certain settings, as the traditional reporting style creates a distance with readers and may be unsuitable for addressing personal-related or emotionally charged topics such as community news and disaster news.
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong

latest_articles.title: More Clickbait, But Fewer Shares? Unpacking the Relationship Between Multimodal Sensationalism and Online User Engagement
latest_articles.abstract: This study examined multimodal sensationalism by analyzing how textual and visual sensationalist features embedded in video headlines and thumbnails relate to user engagement. Using a hybrid human-large language model content analysis, we identified 15 sensationalist features across 1,100 trending videos from Douyin. The results show that legacy news outlets used fewer textual sensationalist elements, particularly Internet slang, hashtags, and positive emotions, than non-journalistic producers. Additionally, visual sensationalist features exhibited an inverted U-shaped relationship with user engagement. These findings advance understanding of the nonlinear and modality-specific effects of sensationalism and offer practical insights into the optimal use of multimodal sensationalism on social media.
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong, China
